Lesson.title: Scoping your landing page before Claude Code writes a line
Lesson.hook: The most expensive hour of this project is the one where you ask Claude Code to “build me a website for my business” and it does. You will get a page. It will look plausible. And you will spend the next three weekends discovering that it takes bookings you do not want, has a blog you will never write, and still does not do the one thing you actually needed — get a message from a stranger into your inbox. The fix costs twenty minutes and no code at all.
Lesson.landing: You now have a written boundary for version one: one page, three things on it, one job it must do. Everything else has a name and a place to wait. That sentence is the first thing you will hand to Claude Code.

sections.text: Scoping is the short conversation you have before any code exists, where you decide what version one of your page is — and, just as importantly, what it is not. For you that is one page, three things on it, and one job: a message from a stranger reaching your inbox.

sections.markdown:
Scoping means fixing the **boundary** before anything gets built. Not a plan, not a spec — a boundary. You write down what the first version contains, what it deliberately leaves out, and the one thing that would make you say “that worked”.

It takes about twenty minutes and it is the only part of this whole project you do entirely without a computer telling you anything.
sections.detail: The reason it comes first is not tidiness. An AI assistant will happily build whatever you describe, at speed, and it has no opinion about whether you needed it. That is a genuinely new problem: the old constraint on building the wrong thing was that building anything was slow and expensive, so you thought first. That constraint is gone. Scoping is what you put in its place — deliberately, because nothing else will do it for you.

sections.markdown: **Scope** is just “what is in and what is out”. When somebody says a project has “scope creep”, they mean things kept quietly getting added until nobody could finish. You will hear the word a lot. It means nothing more complicated than that.

Here is why this matters for **your** page specifically. You said the thing that hurts is that people can only find you by word of mouth. That means version one has exactly one job: somebody who has never met you lands on your page, believes you are real, and gets a message to you without picking up the phone.

A booking system does not do that. A blog does not do that. A newsletter does not do that. They are all good ideas later, and every one of them is a week you are not live.

sections.question: You have an afternoon. Which of these actually belongs in version one of your page?

options.text: A photo of you and three of your work, with a sentence saying what you do
options.feedback: Yes. A stranger has to believe you are a real person who does this. Photos and one honest sentence do that faster than anything else on the page.

options.text: A contact form that sends the message to your inbox
options.feedback: Yes — this is the one job. If everything else on the page were missing and this worked, version one would still have paid for itself.

options.text: A calendar where customers pick a slot and book themselves in
options.feedback: Not yet, and it is the most tempting one. Booking means payments, cancellations, your real availability and somebody being let down when it goes wrong. A form that says “when suits you?” gets you the same customer this month.

options.text: A blog so the page shows up on Google
options.feedback: Later, honestly. A blog only works if you write it every week for months. An empty blog with one post from last March actively makes a business look abandoned.

sections.markdown: Cutting something in this conversation is not giving up on it. It is giving it a date. “Not in version one” and “never” are completely different sentences, and the list you park today is the thing you build next month — on a site that is already earning its keep.

Now the part that is specific to building with AI. You do not scope **at** Claude Code, you scope **with** it — and then you make it repeat the boundary back to you before it touches anything.

The move is simple: describe the business, describe the one job, and ask it to tell you what it thinks version one should contain. Then argue with the answer. It will suggest more than you need, every time, because more is what it has read the most of.

sections.code:
I run a small business on my own and I want a simple one-page website.

The one job of version one: somebody who has never met me lands on the
page, believes I'm real, and sends me a message without phoning.

I have: some photos of my work, and about a paragraph about what I do.
I have never built anything before.

Before writing any code, tell me:
  1. what you think version one should contain, and nothing more
  2. what you'd deliberately leave out, and why
  3. the one assumption you're making that, if it's wrong,
     would change the whole approach

Don't write any code yet. I want to agree the boundary first.
sections.explanation: Paste this, adjusted to your own business, as the very first thing you say. The three numbered questions are the whole technique: the first two give you a boundary, and the third is the one people skip. It is asking the assistant to name what it has quietly assumed — that you want the form to email you rather than store messages somewhere, say — while changing course is still free.

sections.title: Write your boundary down, in one page of plain words
steps: Open a plain note — paper is completely fine for this one.
Write the one job of version one as a single sentence, starting “Somebody who has never met me…”.
Under it, list what is on the page. Stop when you reach four things.
Under that, write “Not yet:” and list everything you just thought of and cut. Give the list a heading and keep it.
Read the one-job sentence out loud. If it contains the word “and” twice, you still have two projects.

capturesProjectFact.prompt: What is the one job of version one, in one sentence?

sections.markdown: **The nasty surprise, and it is not a technical one.** The assistant will never tell you that you are building too much. It has no stake in you finishing. It will accept “actually, can it also do bookings?” with the same enthusiasm it accepted everything else, and three weekends later you will have a half-built booking system and no live website. Nobody will stop that except you, and the boundary you wrote today is how you do it.

One more thing to watch for, and it is the expensive kind because it is hard to undo later: **the assumption nobody says out loud.**

For your page the big one is what happens to a message when somebody presses Send. Email it to you and never store it? Keep every enquiry somewhere you can look back at? Those are different builds, and the second one is much bigger. Decide it now, in a sentence, while the answer is still free.
sections.detail:
The general shape of this: some decisions are cheap to reverse and some are not. Changing a colour, moving a photo, rewording a heading — free, forever. Where your data lives, whether you need somewhere for it to live at all, what your page is actually called on the internet — those get more expensive every week you leave them.

You do not have to get the expensive ones right. You have to get them *decided*, on purpose, instead of discovering that the assistant decided for you in week one and you have been building on it since.

sections.prompt: When somebody presses Send on your form, what should happen to that message?
sections.hint: In your own words. “It should just land in my email” is a complete and very good answer.

sections.title: One page that says what version one is
sections.brief:
Write your scope note — half a page, plain words, no jargon and no code. It should say: the one job of version one; what is on the page; what you have deliberately left for later; and the one assumption that would change everything if it turned out to be wrong.

Write it as though you were handing it to somebody else to build. In a sense you are: this is the first thing you will give Claude Code, and it is what you will hold it to when it suggests something shiny in week two.
rubric: States the one job of version one as a single sentence about a real person doing a real thing
Lists what is on the page, and the list stops at four things or fewer
Has a “not yet” list with at least two things on it that you genuinely wanted
Names at least one assumption that would change the approach if it were wrong
Contains no technical words that you could not explain to a friend

PathStep.rationale: Before Claude Code writes a single line, you and it need to agree what the first version of your page actually is: what a visitor sees, what the contact form asks for, and what is deliberately left until later.
Your page will live on a computer somewhere else, and a visitor's browser will ask it for a copy. That request-and-response picture is what everything else here sits on.

Your photos and your words are the front half; getting a message into your inbox is the back half. Knowing which side owns which job stops you asking for the wrong thing when the form quietly does nothing.
This is the loop you will use for every change to the page: Claude Code says what it intends to do, you read it, then it acts.
Your page is HTML underneath. You will not be writing it, but you will need to read it, because that is how you say the form is missing a field.
The colours, the spacing and whether your page still looks right on a phone are all CSS, and the model is better at it than most people are.
When somebody leaves the email box empty, your form should say so kindly rather than silently doing nothing.
Claude Code will change several files at once and tell you it is done. This is the habit of looking at what really changed before you agree.
At some point your page will come up blank and it will feel like you broke something you do not understand. You have not.
Six questions decide whether this needs to move onto your own computer. For a page that holds photos and keeps an email key secret, the answer is probably yes.
This is the afternoon nobody warns you about: installing the pieces so Claude Code has a real folder to work in.
Once Claude Code is changing several files at a time, you need save points you can go back to.
Claude Code can read, write and run things in your project folder, which is what makes it useful and what makes it easy to lose track of.
Your contact form is the moment your site stops being a page and needs something running elsewhere.
You are not going to build email sending yourself, and you are not going to build photo storage either.
When somebody presses Send, their browser posts what they typed to one particular address that does one job.
Before you tell anybody the site is up: does a message actually reach your inbox? Try it with the email box left empty.
This is where your page stops being on your laptop and starts being somewhere a customer can find it.
Now that the site is live it needs a key to send those emails, and that key must never end up in your code.
You are paying for what Claude Code reads and writes, and most of a bill like yours comes from sending the same things over and over.

ProjectContext.problemStatement: I run a small business on my own, and right now the only way people find me is word of mouth. I want a simple website of my own that says what I do, shows a few photos of my work, and lets someone send me a message without having to phone me.

facts.projectGoal: A single page that explains what my business does, shows photos of my work, and has a contact form that sends the message to my inbox.
facts.buildOrUnderstand: Build it. I want the site to actually exist and be live, not just to understand how websites work.
facts.currentSkillLevel: I have never built anything. I have never written code and I do not really know what a website is made of underneath.
facts.stackOrTools: Claude Code. For hosting I have not chosen yet — somewhere cheap.
facts.whoItIsFor: People within about ten miles who need a bike fixed and currently only find me if a friend passes on my name.
facts.whatTheyveTried: Nothing yet. I looked at the website builders and they seemed either expensive every month or too limiting to look like mine.
facts.worriedAbout: Getting stuck on something technical with nobody to ask. Paying for things I do not need. And not knowing whether what I have built is actually any good, or safe.
facts.versionOneBoundary: Somebody who has never met me finds the page, believes I'm real, and sends me a message about their bike.
facts.whatHappensToAMessage: It should just land in my email. I don't need to keep a list of them anywhere.
facts.coverageArea: About ten miles around town. Further if the weather is good.
facts.scopeNote.oneJob: A stranger with a broken bike gets a message to me without phoning.
facts.scopeNote.whatIsOnThePage: What I do, where I cover, six photos, and the form.
facts.scopeNote.notYet: Online booking, prices, a blog. Not Google **yet** .
facts.ownWords.whatIDo: I fix bicycles at your house, usually the same week.
facts.beFound.searchedFor: "bike repair near me", probably. Richard says to leave this alone for now.

I can see the form in the code but I can't work out which bit is the button.
So is the copy on my computer or theirs?
